title: HLD vs LLD vs Machine Coding

content.title: HLD vs LLD vs Machine Coding

blocks.content: Three rounds, three genuinely different skills being tested. A brilliant architecture with no working code fails a machine coding round. A perfectly compiling program with no thought given to class design fails an LLD round. Showing up to any one of these with the mindset of another is one of the fastest, most common ways to fail an interview that a candidate was otherwise fully capable of clearing.

This topic breaks down exactly what each round tests, what it expects you to produce, how the three connect as one continuous skill zooming from broad to narrow, and the specific trap that sinks candidates in each one.
1. The Three Rounds At a Glance
blocks.text: 1. The Three Rounds At a Glance

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270525788-504513864.png
blocks.alt: The same problem viewed through three different lenses: the whole system, one component, and a working implementation

blocks.content: Think of it as a zoom lens across one continuous skill. High Level Design answers what pieces exist and how they talk to each other. Low Level Design zooms into one of those pieces and asks what classes and objects make it work. Machine Coding takes that same design and demands you actually build it, with real methods, real edge cases, and code that runs.

2. High Level Design In Depth
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025331-195737298.png
blocks.alt: A typical HLD round moves from clarifying requirements through capacity estimation to an architecture diagram, then deeper if pushed

blocks.content: An HLD round tests system level thinking. You never write a single class. The interviewer wants to see you clarify what the system actually needs to do, put rough numbers on scale, storage, and traffic, then lay out the services, databases, and caches that would genuinely handle that scale, along with the trade off behind every major choice.

blocks.title: The Common Trap
blocks.content: Jumping straight to drawing boxes before asking a single clarifying question. An HLD answer built on a wrong assumption about scale or requirements looks confident and is still wrong.
3. Low Level Design In Depth
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270531768-812387717.png
blocks.alt: A typical LLD round moves from identifying entities to relationships to whether a known design pattern genuinely fits

blocks.content: An LLD round zooms all the way into a single component and tests object oriented design judgment. You identify the core entities a system like a parking lot or an elevator control system needs, work out how they relate to each other, and recognize when a known design pattern, Strategy, Observer, Factory, genuinely fits versus when a custom structure is the more honest answer.

blocks.title: The Common Trap
blocks.content: Reaching for a design pattern because it sounds impressive rather than because the problem actually calls for it. An interviewer who asks why you chose a pattern wants a reason rooted in the problem, not the pattern's name.
4. Machine Coding In Depth
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025333-971100572.png
blocks.alt: A machine coding round loops between writing code and fixing edge cases until the tests genuinely pass

blocks.content: A machine coding round is the least forgiving of the three. There is no diagram to gesture at instead of a detail you have not thought through. You design your classes quickly, write code that actually compiles and runs, and the interviewer will hand you inputs specifically chosen to break an implementation that only handles the easy case.

blocks.title: The Common Trap
blocks.content: Spending too long on an elegant class design and running out of time to actually finish working code. A simpler design that fully compiles and handles edge cases beats an elegant one that is half finished.
5. How The Three Connect As One Skill
blocks.text: 5. How The Three Connect As One Skill

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270536344-663154746.png
blocks.alt: The same underlying problem, producing three genuinely different kinds of output depending on which round it is

blocks.content: Low Level Design is essentially the design you would need to have settled before you could machine code a system at all. The difference is that machine coding forces you to commit to every detail a diagram lets you wave away, exactly how a method handles a null input, exactly what happens when two operations race against each other. High Level Design, in turn, is what decides which component even deserves an LLD in the first place.
A diagram can hide an unresolved detail. Running code cannot.
6. The Fastest Way To Fail Each Round
blocks.text: 6. The Fastest Way To Fail Each Round

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785270537977-190717076.png
blocks.alt: Bringing the wrong round's mindset to an HLD interview: writing full implementation code instead of showing the architecture

blocks.content: The single fastest way to fail any of these three rounds is bringing the wrong mindset to it. Writing detailed implementation code in an HLD round burns the entire interview without ever showing the system level thinking that round exists to test. The interviewer is not being unfair by scoring that low, you simply never answered the question they actually asked.
7. The Same Prompt, Three Different Answers
blocks.text: 7. The Same Prompt, Three Different Answers

blocks.title: Design a URL Shortener, Across All Three Rounds
blocks.text: In an HLD round, the answer is a load balancer in front of several application servers, a database sharded by the short code, and a cache in front of it for hot links, with a discussion of how the short code itself gets generated at scale. In an LLD round, the answer is a UrlShortenerService class, a KeyGenerator interface with a swappable base62 encoding strategy, and a UrlRepository interface abstracting the actual storage. In a machine coding round, the answer is all of that, actually implemented, compiling, and correctly returning a working short URL for a real input string within the time limit.

blocks.content: Key Takeaway

HLD, LLD, and Machine Coding are the same underlying design instinct, applied at three different zoom levels and under three different constraints. Knowing which round you are in, and producing exactly the kind of output that round expects, matters as much as the quality of the design itself.
